lead: Some statements fail at run time: a division by zero, a missing dictionary key, a file that is not there. Without a plan, the whole program stops at that line. A try statement lets a block of code declare in advance what to do when a statement inside it fails, and what to do whether it fails or not. One statement carries four parts: try, except, else and finally. Every program that reads input, opens a file or calls a server uses this shape, and so does every library you import.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 (syntax, runtime and semantic errors, tracebacks) and Unit 2 (functions and return values).

blocks.text: Python stops at the first statement that raises an exception (see Unit 1). A try statement changes that. You wrap the risky statements in a try block and write, beside it, the code that should run instead of a crash.
Only the try block is compulsory, but a try with no except and no finally is a SyntaxError, because Python would have nothing to do with the failure.

items: Run the statements of the try block, top to bottom.
If one of them raises, skip the rest of the try block and test the except clauses in the order written.
The first clause whose class matches the exception runs its block, and the exception is then handled.
If no clause matches, the exception leaves the try statement, as if no try existed.
If the try block finished with no exception, the else block runs.
Whatever happened above, the finally block runs last, before control leaves the statement.

blocks.text: The except clause is the exception handler. It names the class of exception it can deal with; the classes themselves are covered in 5.2.

items: One class: except ZeroDivisionError: catches that class and its subclasses.
A tuple: except (ValueError, KeyError): catches any of the listed classes.
With the object: except ValueError as e: binds the exception object to e for that block only; Python deletes the name when the block ends.
Bare: except: with no class catches everything at all.

blocks.text: A bare except is risky. It also catches KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl-C) and SystemExit (raised by sys.exit), so the user cannot stop your program and the program cannot exit. It also hides real bugs behind an empty handler. Write except Exception: when you truly want a wide net.
Order matters. Clauses are tested from the top, so a clause for a base class shadows every later clause for its subclasses. Put the specific classes first.
An exception that no clause matches is not lost. It travels up to the calling function, and if nothing anywhere handles it, the default exception handler prints a traceback and ends the program.

sections.h3: else and finally, and why the order matters

blocks.text: The else block exists for code that must run only when the try block raised nothing. You could put that code at the end of the try block, but then an exception raised by it would be caught by your own except clauses, which were written for something else. In a divide function, printing the quotient belongs in else: a printing bug there should not be reported as a divide-by-zero.

finally runs on every exit from the statement: normal end of try, a handled error, an unhandled error on its way up, a return, a break or continue, or a call to sys.exit(). That makes finally the place for cleanup: closing a file, releasing a lock, deleting a temporary download.
One rule surprises everyone. If finally itself executes return, that return wins and the earlier one is thrown away.
A function may hold a try inside another try. The inner one handles what it recognises, the outer one catches what the inner one let pass, and the inner finally still runs first.

sections.h3: Reading a traceback line by line

blocks.text: When an exception reaches the top unhandled, the default exception handler prints a traceback. Read it from the bottom up.

blocks.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "marks.py", line 7, in <module>
    report(10, 0)
  File "marks.py", line 3, in report
    print(100 / n)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

blocks.text: The last line gives the exception class, ZeroDivisionError, and its message, division by zero. The lines above are the call chain, oldest call first. Each frame holds three facts: the file name in quotes, the line number, and the function that was running, with <module> for top-level code. The source line under each frame shows the exact statement.

Start at the bottom frame: the error happened on line 3 inside report. The frame above says report was called on line 7 of the module. A deeper call chain simply adds more frames. Some syllabi call the except clause the exception handler and the unhandled path the default exception handler; it is the same two mechanisms.

figure.caption: The try block runs first, then the error check sends control to the except block when something was raised and to the else block when nothing was; the finally block runs on both paths.

spec.title: One try statement, four parts
spec.aria: The try block runs, then the error check sends control to the except block when an exception is raised and to the else block when it is not, and the finally block runs in both cases.

examples.question: A function divide is written as shown and called twice, first as divide(10, 2) and then as divide(10, 0). Give the exact output of the whole program in order, and state the final value of q in each call.
steps: First call divide(10, 2): a = 10, b = 2. No statement in the try block raises, so q = 10 / 2 = 5.0.
No exception was raised, so the except clause is skipped and else runs: it prints 'quotient 5.0'.
finally runs: it prints 'done'. q holds 5.0 when the call ends.
Second call divide(10, 0): a = 10, b = 0. The statement q = a / b raises ZeroDivisionError, and the rest of the try block is skipped.
The except clause matches ZeroDivisionError, so it prints 'cannot divide by zero' and sets q = None.
else is skipped, because an exception was raised in the try block.
finally still runs and prints 'done'. q is None when the call ends.
examples.answer: The output is quotient 5.0, done, cannot divide by zero, done, in that order; q is 5.0 after the first call and None after the second.
examples.check:
a, b = 10, 2
q = a / b
print(q)
examples.output:
quotient 5.0
done
cannot divide by zero
done

traps: finally beats return: a return inside try or except is discarded if finally itself returns. The function returns the value from finally.
else is not the code written after the try statement. else runs only when the try block raised nothing; code after the whole try/except/else/finally runs always, even after a handled error.
A bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, so Ctrl-C and sys.exit stop working. except Exception does not catch those two.
A try with neither except nor finally, and a try/else with no except, are SyntaxErrors; examiners like asking which combinations are legal.
Writing a base class (or Exception) as the first clause makes every later clause dead code, because the first matching clause wins.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of a try statement and say which parts are compulsory.
quiz.a: try, except, else, finally. Only try is compulsory, and at least one except or finally clause must be present.

quiz.q: What two things does the last line of a traceback give, and what do the lines above it show?
quiz.a: The last line gives the exception class and its message. The lines above give the call chain, oldest call first, with file name, line number, function name and the failing source line.

quiz.q: Why does Python need an else block, when the same statements could sit at the end of the try block?
quiz.a: Code at the end of the try block is inside the protected region, so any exception it raises would be caught by the except clauses written for the risky statements. else runs only when the try block finished with no exception, so the handler never touches it.

quiz.q: Why is a bare except considered risky, even when the program seems to work?
quiz.a: It catches every exception, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, so the user cannot interrupt the program and the program cannot exit. It also hides bugs, because a wrong statement quietly takes the handler instead of showing a traceback.

quiz.q: Give the exact output: def show(x): try: print(int(x) * 2) except (ValueError, TypeError) as e: print('bad', e) else: print('fine') finally: print('end')  — called as show('7') then show('seven').
quiz.a: show('7') prints 14, then fine, then end. show('seven') raises ValueError inside int(), so it prints bad invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven', skips else, then prints end.

quiz.q: What does this program print? def g(): try: return 1 finally: return 2  print(g())
quiz.a: It prints 2. The return in finally runs on the way out and replaces the pending return 1.

quiz.q: Trace h(0) for: def h(n): try: r = 10 / n except ZeroDivisionError: r = 0; raise else: r = r + 1 finally: print('cleanup'); return r — state what prints and what the caller sees.
quiz.a: 10 / 0 raises ZeroDivisionError, so the except block sets r = 0 and re-raises. else is skipped. finally prints cleanup, and its return r makes the function return 0, so the re-raised exception never reaches the caller. Output: cleanup, and the call evaluates to 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. The with statement (a context manager) gives the same guarantee as finally for files and locks without writing the cleanup yourself, and contextlib lets you build your own. In production code, logging.exception records the full traceback of a handled error instead of printing it. Chained exceptions with raise NewError() from e keep the original cause, and the traceback then shows both. Search for context managers, the logging module and the traceback module next.
